second_order: arguing over tiers, builds, and what works
theme_note: The retained opening thread uses a tier list to compare gods and then turns disagreement into requests, play-style questions, and concrete build substitutions; what varies is whether members contest the ranking or help revise a build.

second_order: doing and undoing April Fools in r/smite
theme_note: These codes all enact, recognize, resist, explain, or clean up the room's own April Fools conduct. The practice ranges from rickrolls and fake changes to the all-Loki makeover, with variation between playing along, objecting, missing the joke, and restoring flairs or the avatar afterward.

second_order: calling people to leave a SMITE mark on the canvas
theme_note: These are direct invitations to make, finish, extend, defend, or join work on SMITE imagery. Calls vary from an initial coordinate and a renewed rally to requests for god art, defenders, and late helpers.

second_order: finding, showing, and claiming the SMITE logo
theme_note: Participants locate the mark, share its current or final state, claim collective authorship, and compare it with nearby marks. What varies is whether the item is a live location report, a disputed survival report, a finished snapshot, or an explanation for a newcomer.

second_order: moving and reshaping the letters to make them read SMITE
theme_note: These codes coordinate concrete layout changes: coordinates, direction, borders, colors, centering, letter widths, and divisions of pixel work. The variation is between proposing a design, correcting it, and announcing a move so helpers do not reverse it.

second_order: keeping the logo standing through repairs and defense
theme_note: These remaining canvas codes share the practical work of preserving a fragile mark: calling out damage, placing repair pixels, dividing defense, conserving dots, and accepting a workable logo. What varies is whether members are repairing a letter, maintaining a border, recruiting defenders, or settling for the design they can hold.

second_order: sorting attacks, jokes, and mistakes from one another
theme_note: The shared practice is attribution under a changing canvas: members inspect histories, accuse vandals or rival groups, admit misclicks, invoke refresh delay, and dispute whether apparent damage was organized. What varies is the proposed culprit and whether the exchange ends in correction, suspicion, or unresolved blame.

second_order: making peace and trading help with canvas neighbours
theme_note: These codes manage shared borders and scarce defenders by warning about claimed space, refusing vandalism, negotiating with r/furry, and asking for reciprocal help from r/furry or r/cloud9. The practice varies between restraint, a claimed permission, a border settlement, and mutual repair promises.

second_order: moving logo work into a megathread, Discord, and an overlay
theme_note: Participants create or request shared coordinating venues, replace expired invites, relay plans back to Reddit, and point helpers to an overlay. What varies is whether the venue is requested, refused then obtained, or only glimpsed through instructions returning to Reddit.

second_order: looking back on an imperfect finish
theme_note: These codes appraise the work after or at the close: participants mourn the ending, celebrate survival and defense, claim repairs, regret mistakes, criticize the M, and share a timelapse. The retrospective ranges from pride and relief to embarrassment and dissatisfaction.

second_order: calling a removed post the Gay Unicorn flag
theme_note: This single surviving title names a possible post-event canvas feature, but its removed body and lack of a human reply leave the referent uncertain; it belongs with no stronger practice.
